How to compute Wasserstein and sliced Wasserstein distances

Source: vignettes/wasserstein-computations.Rmd
wasserstein-computations.Rmd

Goal

This vignette explains how you can use slicer to compute Wasserstein distances between univariate empirical distributions as well as sliced Wasserstein distances between multivariate empirical distributions.

Wasserstein distances between univariate empirical distributions

Let’s first load the slicer package and set a random seed.

library(slicer)
set.seed(20261127)

Given two empirical distributions on ℝ\mathbb{R},

P=1m∑i=1mδxiP = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m \delta_{x_i} and

Q=1n∑j=1nδyj,Q = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \delta_{y_j},

we want to compute the Wasserstein distance of order p∈[1,∞)p \in [1, \infty) between PP and QQ. This is defined as

𝐖p(P,Q):=minX∼PY∼Q(𝔼|X−Y|p)1/p.\mathbf{W}_p(P, Q) := \min_{\substack{X \sim P \\ Y \sim Q}} \left(\mathbb{E}|X - Y|^p\right)^{1/p}.

The distributions PP and QQ are represented as the vectors (or matrices) x=(x1,…,xm)∈ℝm×1x = (x_1, \dots, x_m) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times 1} and y=(y1,…,yn)∈ℝn×1y = (y_1, \dots, y_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}, respectively. For instance,

P <- c(rnorm(20, 14, 3), rnorm(8, 1, 8))
Q <- rcauchy(14, location = 9, scale = 4)

The north-west corner algorithm is used to compute exact Wasserstein distances of order pp. The function nw_corner_distance() runs it.

nw_corner_distance(P, Q, p = 2)
#> [1] 12.35423
nw_corner_distance(P, Q, p = 1)
#> [1] 7.530863

This algorithm is essentially a sorting operation with some bells and whistles. When working with large presorted vectors, you can set the parameter value for presorted to TRUE for some speed-up.

Typically, we will have several empirical distributions P1,…,PNP_1, \dots, P_N. The function compute_all_distances() takes a list of empirical distributions represented as vectors (or matrices). If we don’t specify anything to the contrary, it will assume that the input distributions are all univariate. By default, Wasserstein distances of order p=2p = 2 are computed.

P1 <- P
P2 <- Q
P3 <- rnorm(41)
P4 <- 2*(rbinom(47, 1, 0.4) - 1.5)
pw_dists <- compute_all_distances(list(P1, P2, P3, P4))
#> No projection directions (thetas) supplied. Assuming univariate distributions.
pw_dists
#>          [,1]     [,2]      [,3]      [,4]
#> [1,]  0.00000 12.35423 12.963304 15.023061
#> [2,] 12.35423  0.00000 19.953468 21.676767
#> [3,] 12.96330 19.95347  0.000000  2.252589
#> [4,] 15.02306 21.67677  2.252589  0.000000

Different orders (pp) can be specified, too:

compute_all_distances(list(P1, P2, P3, P4), p = 1)
#> No projection directions (thetas) supplied. Assuming univariate distributions.
#>           [,1]      [,2]      [,3]      [,4]
#> [1,]  0.000000  7.530863 12.059093 14.045166
#> [2,]  7.530863  0.000000 14.134749 16.180809
#> [3,] 12.059093 14.134749  0.000000  2.094052
#> [4,] 14.045166 16.180809  2.094052  0.000000

Wasserstein distances between projected multivariate distributions

While it is possible to define Wasserstein distances between dd-dimensional distributions for d≥2d \geq 2, these distances are expensive to compute. Moreover, they are not Hilbertian. However, what we can do is define a number of vectors θ1,…,θL∈ℝd\theta_1, \dots, \theta_L \in \mathbb{R}^d and compute pp-Wasserstein distances between the projections of the distributions onto these vectors.

More precisely, let P1,…,PNP_1, \dots, P_N be dd-dimensional empirical distributions and let θ1,…,θL\theta_1, \dots, \theta_L be projection vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^d. We now compute

𝐖p(θℓ#⋆Pi,θℓ#⋆Pj)\mathbf{W}_p({\theta_{\ell}}_{\#}^{\star} P_i, {\theta_{\ell}}_{\#}^{\star} P_j) for all ℓ=1,…,L,1≤i<j≤N\ell = 1, \dots, L, 1 \leq i < j \leq N, where v#⋆Qv_{\#}^{\star}Q is the pushforward (image) measure of QQ under the map x↦v⊤xx \mapsto v^{\top}x.

Using slicer, we can compute these L⋅N(N−1)/2L \cdot N(N-1)/2 pairwise distances as follows. We represent each dd-dimensional empirical distribution

Pi=1ni∑k=1niδxi,k,P_i = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{k = 1}^{n_i} \delta_{x_{i, k}}, with xi,k∈ℝdx_{i,k} \in \mathbb{R}^d, as a matrix,

Mi=(xi,1⊤⋮xi,ni⊤)∈ℝni×d.M_i = \begin{pmatrix} x^{\top}_{i, 1} \\ \vdots \\ x^{\top}_{i, n_i} \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i \times d}.

We put these matrices M1,…,MNM_1, \dots, M_N in a list.

Then, we define a matrix

Θ=(θ1⊤⋮θL⊤)∈ℝL×d\Theta = \begin{pmatrix} \theta^{\top}_1 \\ \vdots \\ \theta^{\top}_L \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d} that contains the projection vectors. If we’re just interested in obtaining Wasserstein distances between the corresponding marginal distributions, we set Θ=Id\Theta = I_d.

Then, we feed the list of MM-matrices and Θ\Theta to compute_all_distances().

By way of example, we generate a number (NN) of samples from different Gaussian mixtures with a randomly chosen number of components cUnif(1,2,…,C)c ~ \textrm{Unif}(1, 2, \dots, C) using the following code.

rgmm_random <- function(n, C, d) {
  p <- sample.int(C, 1) 
  mu <- matrix(runif(p * d, -5, 5), nrow = p, ncol = d)
  chol_list <- lapply(seq_len(p), function(j) {
    a <- runif(1, 1, 4)
    A <- matrix(runif(d * d, -1, 1), d, d)
    B <- diag(runif(d, 0, 1), nrow = d)
    Sigma <- a * tcrossprod(A) + B
    chol(Sigma)       
  })
  z <- sample.int(p, n, replace = TRUE)
  X <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = d)
  for (j in seq_len(p)) {
    idx <- which(z == j)
    m <- length(idx)
    if (m > 0) {
      Z <- matrix(rnorm(m * d), m, d)
      X[idx, ] <- Z %*% chol_list[[j]] +
        matrix(mu[j, ], m, d, byrow = TRUE)
    }
  }
  list(distribution = X, components = p)
}
rgmm_random_N <- function(N = 100, n = 50, C = 4, d = 8) {
  replicate(N, rgmm_random(n, C, d), simplify = FALSE)
}

We generate N=6N = 6 8-dimensional empirical distributions by drawing samples of size n=500n = 500 from Gaussian mixture models with between 1 and C=4C = 4 mixture components. (It is not necessary for the distributions to be supported on the same number of points.)

rgmms <- rgmm_random_N(N = 6, n = 500, C = 4, d = 8)
distributions <- lapply(rgmms, `[[`, "distribution")

If we want to compute the pairwise Wasserstein distances between the corresponding margins (i.e., after projecting the distributions onto each of the cardinal axes) as well as those between the projections onto, say, the vector

θ9=13(0,1,0,1,0,0,0,1)⊤,\theta_9 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1)^{\top}, then we put the canonical basis vectors e1,…,e8e_1, \dots, e_8 as well as θ9\theta_9 into a matrix:

Theta <- rbind(
  diag(1, 8),
  1/sqrt(3) * c(0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1)
)
Theta
#>       [,1]      [,2] [,3]      [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7]      [,8]
#>  [1,]    1 0.0000000    0 0.0000000    0    0    0 0.0000000
#>  [2,]    0 1.0000000    0 0.0000000    0    0    0 0.0000000
#>  [3,]    0 0.0000000    1 0.0000000    0    0    0 0.0000000
#>  [4,]    0 0.0000000    0 1.0000000    0    0    0 0.0000000
#>  [5,]    0 0.0000000    0 0.0000000    1    0    0 0.0000000
#>  [6,]    0 0.0000000    0 0.0000000    0    1    0 0.0000000
#>  [7,]    0 0.0000000    0 0.0000000    0    0    1 0.0000000
#>  [8,]    0 0.0000000    0 0.0000000    0    0    0 1.0000000
#>  [9,]    0 0.5773503    0 0.5773503    0    0    0 0.5773503

The squared 2-Wasserstein distances between the projections onto each row of Theta can now be computed as follows:

all_dists <- compute_all_distances(distributions, Theta)
#> Projecting...
#> Computing distances...
#>   |                                                                              |                                                                      |   0%  |                                                                              |========                                                              |  11%  |                                                                              |================                                                      |  22%  |                                                                              |=======================                                               |  33%  |                                                                              |===============================                                       |  44%  |                                                                              |=======================================                               |  56%  |                                                                              |===============================================                       |  67%  |                                                                              |======================================================                |  78%  |                                                                              |==============================================================        |  89%  |                                                                              |======================================================================| 100%

The object all_dists is a list with 9 elements (the number of projection directions), each of which contains Wasserstein distances of order p=2p = 2:

# Along fourth canonical basis vector
all_dists[[4]]
#>          [,1]     [,2]      [,3]     [,4]      [,5]     [,6]
#> [1,] 0.000000 2.511518 2.3869818 3.511217 2.5519653 1.079536
#> [2,] 2.511518 0.000000 4.1255069 5.956054 4.6548244 3.089585
#> [3,] 2.386982 4.125507 0.0000000 2.837708 0.9174726 1.379150
#> [4,] 3.511217 5.956054 2.8377080 0.000000 2.0281511 3.005094
#> [5,] 2.551965 4.654824 0.9174726 2.028151 0.0000000 1.615499
#> [6,] 1.079536 3.089585 1.3791504 3.005094 1.6154990 0.000000

# Along theta_9
all_dists[[9]]
#>          [,1]     [,2]     [,3]     [,4]     [,5]     [,6]
#> [1,] 0.000000 2.135175 1.975174 4.061653 2.578371 1.765189
#> [2,] 2.135175 0.000000 2.176853 5.892668 3.707649 2.853606
#> [3,] 1.975174 2.176853 0.000000 4.348005 1.969027 1.420678
#> [4,] 4.061653 5.892668 4.348005 0.000000 2.737301 3.201242

Sliced Wasserstein distances

To estimate sliced Wasserstein distances between dd-variate empirical probability distributions, we generate independent θ1,…,θL\theta_1, \dots, \theta_L uniformly at random from the unit sphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^d. The function generate_directions() takes care of this:

Theta <- generate_directions(L = 50, d = 8)

We again use compute_all_distances() but set the average parameter to TRUE. The function now averages the LL Wasserstein distances computed for each pair of distributions like so:

𝐒𝐖̂p(Pi,Pj)=(1L∑ℓ=1L𝐖pp(θℓ#⋆Pi,θℓ#⋆Pj))1/p.\widehat{\mathbf{SW}}_p(P_i, P_j) = \left(\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell = 1}^L \mathbf{W}^p_p({\theta_{\ell}}_{\#}^{\star} P_i, {\theta_{\ell}}_{\#}^{\star} P_j)\right)^{1/p}. By default, squared sliced Wasserstein distances of order p=2p = 2 are output:

sw_dists <- compute_all_distances(distributions, Theta, average = TRUE)
#> Projecting...
#> Computing distances...
